questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that is safe because nothing could count against it
questions.learningObjective: Identify a thesis that no possible evidence could refute
questions.stem: A dispatcher's seminar paper argues that service reliability must always be improved and that no timetable should ever be treated as final. Which judgement best describes this thesis?

options.text: It is safe because nothing can count against it, so no evidence could ever test it.
It is safe because every transport regulator agrees that reliability comes before punctuality.
options.misconception: cites agreement in place of a testable claim

options.text: It is safe because it takes both sides of the reliability question and cannot be wrong.
options.misconception: mistakes balance for the absence of any commitment

options.text: It is safe because the dispatcher commits to improving reliability without fixing any target.
options.misconception: treats the absence of a measure as a strength

questions.explanation: A thesis that permits no exception cannot be contradicted, so no evidence bears on it. That safety is the problem: no possible finding could change the claim, so the reader learns nothing from it.
questions.hint: Ask what result could prove the thesis wrong.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that reports accurately and stops there
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of an accurate but unjudged response
questions.stem: A dispatcher's response to a book on timetable reliability summarises every chapter accurately and ends without any evaluation. In two or three sentences, explain what this response can and cannot do for the seminar.

answer.exemplar: The response gives an accurate account of what the book argues, which is useful as a map of the field. It cannot do the work of a seminar contribution, because it leaves the reader with no view to weigh, nothing to disagree with, and no basis for deciding whether the account suits the dispatcher's own operating context.

questions.explanation: An accurate report transfers the source's content without adding the writer's assessment. The seminar needs the writer's view, since without one there is nothing for the group to test.
questions.hint: Say what the writer thinks, not only what the book says.

stimulus.body: This book is very well organised and easy to read. questions.stem: Which statement best describes what this response does?

options.text: It reports the book's content and also judges it against the writer's own experience.
It reports the book's content accurately and adds no evaluation of it.
options.misconception: misses the writer's stated agreement with the author

options.text: It evaluates the book but gives almost no account of what the book actually says.
options.misconception: describes a summary as an evaluation

options.text: It gives a hostile account of the book in order to defend the roster already in use.
options.misconception: assumes disagreement is required for a judgement

questions.explanation: A response that reports and judges contains both an account of the source and the writer's assessment of it. Here the disagreement is with the author's framing, which is what judgement permits.
questions.hint: Look for the writer's own experience being used.

questions.stem: A dispatcher's thesis says that signalling modernisation always improves punctuality. Which rewrite makes the thesis answerable?

options.text: Signalling modernisation always improves punctuality and always will do so.
options.misconception: repeats the absolute rather than narrowing it

options.text: Signalling modernisation improves punctuality, which everyone in the industry agrees.
options.misconception: adds an appeal to consensus instead of a scope

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A review comment a writer can act on
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a review comment actionable
questions.stem: A reviewer writes: the second paragraph needs a source for the delay figure, and it should say which lines the figure covers. In two or three sentences, explain why this comment is usable by the writer.

answer.exemplar: The comment names a specific place in the draft, a specific omission, and the action that would fix it, so the writer can act without guessing at what the reviewer meant. A usable comment is not merely negative; it gives the writer something concrete to do and a way to judge whether the revision has worked.

questions.explanation: A comment is actionable when it locates the problem, names what is missing, and points at the remedy. Praise or general discouragement tells the writer nothing about what to change or how.
questions.hint: Ask whether the writer knows what to change next.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that is interesting and cannot be settled
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a wide opening question can become workable
questions.stem: A dispatcher's seminar paper opens with a wide question about how operators should handle disruption that no one can yet measure. In two or three sentences, explain how the writer could make such an opening usable.

answer.exemplar: The writer can keep the large question but attach it to a narrower one that the available records could bear on, such as which measures dispatchers already use to restore a service after a signal failure. That lets the paper move the discussion forward without claiming to have settled the wider problem, which no evidence could do.

questions.explanation: A broad question can be honest and still be unworkable, because no result could count as progress towards it. Anchoring it to a narrower question keeps the research reachable.
questions.hint: Attach the wide question to one that evidence can move.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that is safe because nothing could count against it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unconditional thesis resists testing
questions.stem: Signalling investment, the thesis says, should always be prioritised over rolling stock. In two or three sentences, explain why this thesis is hard to test.

answer.exemplar: The thesis allows no circumstance in which rolling stock would come first, so no record of what a depot actually spent could count against it. questions.stem: A reviewer tells a dispatcher that the argument in section two is sound but the timetable data behind it is wrong. In two or three sentences, explain what makes this comment usable and what it still leaves open.

answer.exemplar: The comment separates the two things a writer can act on: the reasoning is endorsed, so it need not be rewritten, while the data is identified as faulty, so it must be checked and replaced. questions.stem: A dispatcher writes that a book on train formation is wrong to ignore how formations are actually built at depots. In two or three sentences, explain what the dispatcher needs for this to count as a response rather than an objection.

answer.exemplar: The dispatcher needs to say what the book claims, accurately and in enough detail that the disagreement can be located, and then to give the depot practice that shows the claim to be unsafe. stimulus.body: A dispatcher's seminar thesis asks: can an operating railway be run without a printed timetable at all, and what would the crews, the controllers and the passengers lose if it were?

questions.stem: What is the most constructive response to this thesis?

options.text: Reject it, because a thesis must make a claim that can be proved within one term.
options.misconception: imposes a deadline on what a question may ask

options.text: Rewrite it to argue that printed timetables are unnecessary, which is easier to assess.
options.misconception: converts the question into the conclusion the writer wants

options.text: Accept it unchanged, because a wide question is the sign of a confident writer.
options.misconception: treats breadth as a mark of quality

options.text: Keep the question and frame it around what evidence could support or defeat each part.

questions.explanation: A wide question is valuable when it can be broken into parts that evidence can bear on. Rewriting it into the conclusion the writer prefers avoids the research the question invites.
questions.hint: Break the question into parts evidence could answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that cannot be stated in one sentence
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose and fix a thesis that resists compression
questions.stem: A dispatcher cannot reduce a thesis about depot stabling to a single sentence. In two or three sentences, explain what to do about that difficulty.

answer.exemplar: The dispatcher should ask whether the difficulty lies in the claim or in its presentation. If there is one claim, it can be stated plainly with the qualifications moved into subordinate positions, and if there are several claims, the paper should say so and choose which one it will argue. The trouble is rarely the length of the sentence.

questions.explanation: A thesis that resists one sentence usually hides more than one claim, or one claim buried under qualifications. Separating the claim from its conditions reveals which problem is present.
questions.hint: Ask whether you have one claim or several.

questions.learningObjective: Find a workable research question inside an experiential thesis

options.misconception: assumes such research is impossible rather than difficult

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rewriting a thesis so it could be answered
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an absolute thesis can be rewritten for testing
questions.stem: A dispatcher's thesis states that better signalling always produces better punctuality. In two or three sentences, explain how the writer could rewrite it so it could be answered.

answer.exemplar: The writer could restrict the claim to corridors where the existing signalling is the binding constraint and state the measure of punctuality to be used, then frame the thesis as a question about whether the investment produces a measurable gain in that setting. The rewritten claim would be capable of being shown wrong by records that already exist.

questions.explanation: A thesis becomes answerable when it is bounded and phrased so a finding could go against it. The rewrite turns an assertion into something the available records can settle.
questions.hint: Bound the claim and name the finding that would defeat it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that reports accurately and stops there
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a seminar loses from an unjudged response
questions.stem: A dispatcher's seminar response reports a book on delay attribution accurately and then stops. In two or three sentences, explain what the seminar loses from that response as it stands.

answer.exemplar: The seminar gains an accurate map of what the book argues, which is worth having when members have not read it. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A review comment addressed to the person
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a personal remark from a substantive review point
questions.stem: A reviewer's remark says the dispatcher's chapter is written by someone who has never been on a platform at rush hour, and it shows in the way crowding is described. Which judgement is fairest?

options.text: The comment is fair, because insider experience is the only basis for describing crowding.
options.misconception: makes experience the sole legitimate ground of description

options.text: The comment is fair, because the author's lack of experience is visible in the prose.
options.misconception: accepts a remark about style as evidence about the argument

options.text: The comment is incomplete, because it should name the passage where the description fails.
options.misconception: misses the deeper fault, which is the attack on the writer

options.text: The comment is unusable, because it judges the writer rather than the description.

questions.explanation: The fault is the target, not the tone: a remark about the writer's career cannot be answered by revising the paper. It becomes usable once it points at the passage that falls short.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comment points at the paper or the person.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that cannot be stated in one sentence
questions.learningObjective: Separate two claims hidden inside a single thesis
questions.stem: A dispatcher's thesis cannot be stated in one sentence because the writer has put a second claim inside it about the effects on passengers. What is the best correction?

options.text: Join the two claims with a semicolon so that the sentence stays long but reads as one.
options.misconception: keeps two claims in one sentence without separating them

options.text: Split the claims and state which one the paper will argue.
Cut the passenger claim, since it is a matter of opinion rather than argument.
options.misconception: dismisses a claim on grounds of its subject matter

options.text: Move the passenger claim into the introduction, where it will do no harm.
options.misconception: relocates the problem rather than solving it

questions.explanation: Two claims in one thesis cannot be argued clearly, because the evidence for one is not evidence for the other. Separating them and choosing which to pursue is the smallest fix.
questions.hint: Ask which claim the paper is actually about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that is safe because nothing could count against it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unqualified moral thesis resists testing
questions.stem: A dispatcher's seminar thesis says that passengers should always be told the truth about why their train is late. In two or three sentences, explain why this claim is hard to test and how it could be made testable.

answer.exemplar: The claim allows no circumstance in which another form of announcement would be better, so no comparison of passenger reactions could count against it. It could be made testable by specifying the announcements being compared, the context, and the measure of whether passengers were helped, and by allowing for cases where a partial truth served them better.

questions.explanation: A claim that always holds cannot be checked against the records of what actually happened. Naming the alternatives it excludes turns a safe assertion into a question.
questions.hint: Ask what alternative the claim excludes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that reports accurately and stops there
questions.learningObjective: Choose the addition that completes a descriptive response

stimulus.body: A dispatcher's response to a book on passenger information is accurate throughout and describes the author's findings on when announcements are made. The response adds no view of its own.

questions.stem: What is the most useful next step for the dispatcher?

options.text: Rewrite the response to criticise the author's method, since agreement alone adds nothing.
options.misconception: prescribes hostility as the only alternative to summary

options.text: Add more detail from the book so that the account becomes more useful to the group.
options.misconception: mistakes more detail for the missing judgement

options.text: Add a paragraph stating where the writer agrees and where the writer thinks the author overreaches.
Ask the author of the book to join the seminar and answer for the findings directly.
options.misconception: sends the question to the source instead of adding a view

questions.explanation: The missing element is the writer's own assessment, which is what turns an accurate account into a contribution. Criticism and further detail leave the judgement where it was.
questions.hint: Add the view the response currently keeps back.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that reports and judges
questions.learningObjective: Preserve and sharpen a specific reservation about a source
questions.stem: A dispatcher summarises a book on timetable recovery, then remarks that its three principles assume a junction the writer has never seen. Which revision best serves the seminar?

options.text: Remove the remark, since doubts about an unseen junction weaken the response.
options.misconception: treats a genuine reservation as damage

options.text: Keep the remark and say what the principles would need in order to work at the writer's junction.
Replace the remark with a fuller summary of the three principles for the group's benefit.
options.misconception: trades the judgement for more summary

options.text: Move the remark to a footnote so the body of the response stays clean.
options.misconception: hides the reservation instead of using it

questions.explanation: A specific reservation about the source's assumptions is useful because it is located and can be acted on. Removing it or tucking it into a note discards what a working group needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the principles would need in order to work here.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that is interesting and cannot be settled
questions.learningObjective: Keep a plausible explanation in a form evidence could settle
questions.stem: A dispatcher's seminar thesis argues that the reason punctuality falls on Sundays is that the timetable is designed for commuters. Which course of action best serves the paper?

options.text: Publish the thesis as it stands, since the explanation is well established in the trade.
options.misconception: treats trade consensus as the evidence a thesis needs

options.text: Broaden the thesis to all off-peak services, so that the Sunday case becomes one example of many.
options.misconception: widens the claim rather than testing it

options.text: Drop the thesis, since a single day of the week cannot support any conclusion.
options.misconception: rejects a workable claim on a technicality

options.text: Keep the claim but frame it as a question the Sunday and weekday data could answer.

questions.explanation: A specific and plausible explanation is worth keeping, provided it is framed so the timetables and ridership data could test it. Publishing it as settled avoids that comparison.
questions.hint: Ask whether the Sunday and weekday data could settle it.
